title: Real space and represented space: Cross-cultural perspectives
central_proposition: Cross-cultural studies reveal that the perception and representation of space involve distinct types of skills—some related exclusively to real space, some to represented space, and some shared—which vary in acquisition and application across different cultural groups and stimuli.

concept_definitions.name: 2D images without direct three-dimensional cues (2/3i)
concept_definitions.definition: Images containing cues that lead indirectly to the recognition of a three-dimensional object without evoking the illusion of space, where perception of spatial attributes is modified by object recognition.

concept_definitions.name: 2D images with direct 3D cues (2/3d)
concept_definitions.definition: Images that evoke the illusion of space directly, often representing objects with readily perceptible three-dimensional quality, even if impossible.

concept_definitions.name: 3D spatial skills
concept_definitions.definition: Perceptual skills used in dealing with the real world, such as judging distance by binocular disparity or interpreting overlap.

concept_definitions.name: Representational skills
concept_definitions.definition: Perceptual skills used to make optimum use of pictures, including interpreting multiple representations as depicting movement or recognizing stick figures as men.

concept_definitions.name: Carpentered world hypothesis
concept_definitions.definition: The proposition that subjects from environments with many solid right angles are more prone to geometric illusions (e.g., Müller-Lyer) due to a habit of interpreting ambiguous angles as right angles.

concept_definitions.name: Ecological hypothesis
concept_definitions.definition: The proposition that inhabitants of open terrain are more likely to interpret ambiguous linear stimuli as extending away from them, making them more susceptible to the horizontal-vertical illusion.

concept_definitions.name: Type of Array
concept_definitions.definition: A factor describing how elements of a display are structured, ranging from anarchic (separate, unrelated entities) to totalitarian (all elements integrated for recognition).

concept_definitions.name: Figure/Background Separation
concept_definitions.definition: A factor describing the ease of detecting a figure in a display, ranging from difficult (figure embedded in noise) to easy (figure clearly distinguishable).

concept_definitions.name: Implicit shape constancy
concept_definitions.definition: The tendency to perceive a shape as constant despite changes in its retinal projection, influenced by background cues.

concept_definitions.name: Secondary awareness
concept_definitions.definition: The observer's awareness of the perceptual significance of the pictorial surface, crucial for perceiving pictures with strong depth impressions.

argument_structure: The paper reviews extensive cross-cultural and some animal studies on picture perception and visual illusions. It identifies inconsistencies and limitations in previous research, then proposes a conceptual framework distinguishing two kinds of images (2/3i and 2/3d) and two categories of perceptual skills (real space and representational space, with overlap). It argues that cultural and experiential factors influence the acquisition and application of these skills, leading to observed cross-cultural differences in how pictures are perceived and interpreted.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is that perceptual skills, acquired through experience in the real world, are transferred to and modified by experience with pictures. The effectiveness of this transfer depends on the similarity of cues processed in real vs. represented space, the specific type of picture (2/3i vs. 2/3d), and cultural learning that assigns different importance to various cues. Difficulties arise from a mismatch between learned cue systems and the cues presented in culturally alien pictures, or from a lack of integration of pictorial elements.

findings.antecedent: Pictorial space
findings.mechanism: Visual cues (e.g., density gradients) used for distance perception in real space can also create illusions in pictures, indicating a fundamental perceptual link.
findings.quote: pictorial space is... a derivative of real space.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Jerison (1967) on trapezoid illusion, Opolot (1976) on distance judgments.

findings.antecedent: Picture's surface
findings.mechanism: The surface of a picture can be perceived as defining an 'inside' space (for spatial layout) and an 'outside' space (for object rotation), suggesting distinct perceptual processing for different aspects of pictorial information.
findings.quote: picture's surface defines two types of pictorial space: one inside and one outside the picture.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Goldstein (1979), Deregowski and Parker (1988).

findings.antecedent: 2D images with direct 3D cues (2/3d figures)
findings.mechanism: These images contain configurations of lines and gradients that directly trigger the perceptual system's interpretation of three-dimensionality, often without requiring object recognition.
findings.quote: they may evoke the illusion of space directly
findings.empirical_support_cited: Impossible figures (two-pronged trident, Reutersvard's triangle), truncated pyramid.

findings.antecedent: 2D images without direct three-dimensional cues (2/3i figures)
findings.consequent: Perception of spatial attributes of the object
findings.mechanism: For these figures, the recognition of the represented object (e.g., elephant silhouette) provides the context that allows the perceptual system to infer or modify the spatial attributes, rather than the image directly conveying 3D space.
findings.quote: perception of the spatial attributes of the object is modified by the recognition of the object
findings.empirical_support_cited: Elephant silhouette, Tallensi stick figures.

findings.antecedent: Ambiguous patterns (e.g., Rubin vase, Palaeolithic engraving)
findings.mechanism: The perceptual system attempts to 'make sense' of stimuli by creating 3D objects, even when the stimuli are ambiguous or impossible, demonstrating a strong drive to interpret visual input in three-dimensional terms.
findings.quote: ambiguous patterns... are readily perceived and have provided substance for much discussion by Gestalt psychologists
findings.empirical_support_cited: Petermann (1932), Rubin (1915) on ambiguous figures; Kulpa (1983, 1987) on truncated pyramid.

findings.antecedent: Flat figures (individually seen as having no pictorial depth) in combination (e.g., two similar figures of different size at different heights)
findings.mechanism: The relative size and elevation cues, similar to those responsible for the Ponzo illusion, are interpreted by the perceptual system to infer depth, with the more elevated figure seen as more distant.
findings.quote: Even flat figures... can in combination create three-dimensional pictorial space.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ponzo illusion (Figure 8) and its derivatives.

findings.antecedent: Lack of experience with pictures
findings.mechanism: Observers with limited pictorial experience may fail to recognize pictures as representations, misidentify objects, or struggle to integrate elements, suggesting that picture perception is a learned skill.
findings.quote: errors made by subjects with limited experience with pictures
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortes (1940, 1981) on Tallensi, Deregowski et al. (1972) on Me'en, Doob (1961) on Fulani, Cole and Scribner (1974) on Kpelle, Barley (1986) on Dowayos.

findings.antecedent: Dominant influence of the material on which pictures are presented (when culturally alien)
findings.consequent: Failure to make sense of the surface pattern
findings.mechanism: When the medium itself is novel or unfamiliar, observers' attention is directed to the material rather than the depicted content, hindering pictorial perception.
findings.quote: This dominant influence of the material on which pictures are presented is similar to a much earlier finding
findings.empirical_support_cited: Deregowski et al. (1972) on Me'en (paper vs. coarse cloth), Nadel (1939/1946) on Yoruba (paper vs. leatherwork).

findings.antecedent: Reducing the influence of nonpictorial cues (e.g., novelty of material)
findings.mechanism: When distractions related to the picture's physical properties or context are minimized, observers can better attend to and interpret the pictorial content, sometimes leading to dramatic recognition.
findings.quote: reducing the influence of the nonpictorial cues greatly enhances perception by the pictorially unsophisticated
findings.empirical_support_cited: Lloyd (1904) on Ugandan slide show (elephant).

findings.antecedent: Mismatch between observer's expectation and what is actually encountered in a picture
findings.consequent: Failure to see relatives in photographs
findings.mechanism: Lack of expertise in interpreting pictorial conventions (e.g., rigid poses vs. workday postures) can lead to disappointment and inability to recognize familiar subjects in photographs.
findings.quote: mismatch between the expectation and what is actually encountered, for which lack of expertise is responsible.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Forge (1970) on New Guinea informants.

findings.antecedent: Pictures with scattered elements (anarchic) or embedded figures (highly embedded)
findings.mechanism: The perceptual system struggles to integrate disparate elements or disentangle figures from irrelevant detail, leading to problems in recognizing the depicted object.
findings.quote: difficulties some observers from pictorially sophisticated cultures experience when asked to disembed a figure from a mass of visual noise
findings.empirical_support_cited: Street figure (Figure 13), Witkin's Embedded Figures Test (Figure 14a), Ghent (1956) overlapping figures (Figure 14c), Berry (1966).

findings.antecedent: Stimuli with elements taken in isolation (e.g., Shaw's tortoise, Binet's syncretic animals)
findings.consequent: Misidentification or naming of individual parts
findings.mechanism: When observers fail to integrate pictorial elements into a coherent whole, they may focus on salient individual parts, leading to incorrect or partial recognition.
findings.quote: Shaw's subjects saw the figure as less well integrated (i. e., more anarchic) than either he or the draughtsman thought it was
findings.empirical_support_cited: Binet (1890) on 'syncretic' animals, Elkind (1969) on fruit face, Shaw (1969) on tortoise (Figure 16), Ausburn and Ausburn (1983) on Matching Familiar Figures.

findings.antecedent: Perception of impossible figures (e.g., two-pronged trident) as 2/3d
findings.mechanism: When subjects perceive the spatial properties of an impossible figure, they become aware of its inherent contradictions, making the task of accurately reproducing it more difficult than simply copying a flat pattern.
findings.quote: Those who perceived the pictures as 2/3d, and constructed 3D models, took relatively longer to copy the 'two-pronged trident' figure than those who built flat models.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Deregowski (1969) on Zambian schoolchildren copying trident.

findings.antecedent: Cultural differences in carpentered environments
findings.mechanism: The 'carpentered world hypothesis' suggests that exposure to rectangular artifacts leads to a habit of interpreting obtuse/acute angles as right angles, making individuals more prone to the illusion due to constancy scaling.
findings.quote: inhabitants of open terrain... more susceptible to the horizontal-vertical illusion
findings.empirical_support_cited: Segall et al. (1963, 1966), Laws (1886), Berry (1968), Ahluwalia (1978).

findings.antecedent: Cultural differences in open terrain environments
findings.mechanism: The 'ecological hypothesis' suggests that inhabitants of open terrain are more likely to interpret ambiguous linear stimuli as extending away, making them more prone to the illusion because the upright arm is seen as extending away and hence longer.
findings.quote: inhabitants of open terrain... more susceptible to the horizontal-vertical illusion
findings.empirical_support_cited: Segall et al. (1963, 1966).

findings.antecedent: Universality of illusions (illusion-evoking stimuli are 2/3d)
findings.consequent: Universality of 2/3d perception of illusion-evoking elements
findings.mechanism: If illusions arise because figures evoke 3D percepts, and illusions are universally experienced (though with cultural variation in intensity), then the basic perception of 2/3d figures must also be universal.
findings.quote: universality of illusions argues for the universality of 2/3d perception of those figures that incorporate illusion-evoking elements.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Segall et al. (1966), Gregory (1973).

findings.antecedent: Cultural differences in the way pictures are treated (even when correctly labelled)
findings.mechanism: Beyond basic recognition, cultural norms and experiences influence how observers interact with and interpret pictorial information, leading to variations in how they process and respond to pictures.
findings.quote: Hence there is evidence of cultural differences in the way pictures are treated, even when they are correctly labelled.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Perkins & Deregowski (1982) on sorting blocks vs. pictures, Deregowski (1971a) on matching tasks, Deregowski & Jahoda (1975) on learning tasks, Sigel (1968, 1978) on Piagetian sorting, Deregowski & Serpell (1971) on sorting objects/photographs, Ramkissoon & Bhana (1982).

findings.antecedent: Flat background indicating 'picture as picture'
findings.mechanism: The awareness of the pictorial surface as flat provides a crucial contextual cue that allows the observer to interpret the array of lines and shapes as a three-dimensional representation rather than a real object.
findings.quote: Two factors therefore contribute to the recognition of such a figure as 2/3d, first, the flat background that indicates to the observer that the array can be interpreted as a 2/3d one
findings.empirical_support_cited: Pirenne (1970) on Pozzo ceilings, Gregory (1970) on luminous models, Muldrow and Muldrow (Deregowski et al. 1972), Serpell and Deregowski (1980).

findings.antecedent: Nature of the figure (e.g., specific depth cues)
findings.mechanism: The intrinsic properties and arrangement of elements within the figure itself provide cues that ensure a three-dimensional interpretation, independent of the background context.
findings.quote: second, the nature of the figure that ensures such an interpretation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Pirenne (1970) on Pozzo ceilings, Gregory (1970) on luminous models, Muldrow and Muldrow (Deregowski et al. 1972), Serpell and Deregowski (1980).

findings.antecedent: Cultural differences in carpentered environments (e.g., tribal origin, exposure)
findings.mechanism: Experience with carpentered environments influences how observers perceive and interpret depth cues, leading to variations in the perceived sizes of objects in the Ames room.
findings.quote: The scores of various subsamples of the Zambian sample... showed a trend consistent with the carpentered world hypothesis
findings.empirical_support_cited: Stewart (1973) on North American and Zambian subjects.

findings.antecedent: Different perceptual skills
findings.mechanism: Observers may employ different strategies, such as field-dependent (comparing objects to aspects of the field) or field-independent (relying on binocular convergence), when assessing perceptual constancies.
findings.quote: different perceptual skills can be used when judging constancies
findings.empirical_support_cited: Van de Koppel (1983) on size constancy and field dependence.

findings.antecedent: Observers' learning of relative importance of perceptual cues in real space
findings.consequent: Learning subsequently modified in experiencing pictures
findings.mechanism: The perceptual system adapts its cue weighting based on real-world experience, and this learned system is then further refined or altered through exposure to and interpretation of pictorial representations.
findings.quote: observers learn the relative importance of various perceptual cues in the context of real space, and that that learning is subsequently modified in experiencing pictures.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Brislin & Keating (1976) on Ponzo illusion in pictures vs. 3D objects.

findings.antecedent: Same perceptual skills
findings.consequent: Dealing with the real world and with pictures
findings.mechanism: The underlying perceptual mechanisms for processing spatial cues are shared between real and represented spaces, allowing for transfer of 3D spatial skills into the realm of pictures.
findings.quote: the same perceptual skills are used in dealing with the real world and in dealing with pictures.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Brislin & Keating (1976) on Ponzo illusion in pictures vs. 3D objects.

findings.antecedent: Skills appropriate to the perception of real space
findings.mechanism: Observers proficient in real-world spatial perception can effectively apply these skills to interpret pictorial space, especially for tasks that involve direct transfer of 3D spatial understanding.
findings.quote: Observers who perform well on real space... will also perform well on picture tasks that can be accomplished with the skills appropriate to the perception of real space.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Colomb & Dasen (1986) on Baoule children's spatial tasks and drawing comprehension.

findings.antecedent: Lack of purely representational skills OR limited expertise with real-space skills relevant to picture perception
findings.mechanism: Deficiencies in either picture-specific interpretive abilities or the foundational real-world spatial skills necessary for picture interpretation can hinder an observer's ability to comprehend represented space.
findings.quote: poor understanding of representational space may either be a consequence of lacking purely representational skills or of limited expertise with real-space skills relevant to picture perception.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortes (1940), Hudson (1960), Perkins & Deregowski (1982).

findings.antecedent: Cultural climate (e.g., questions about 'What are things really like?')
findings.consequent: Style of painting and other arts
findings.mechanism: The prevailing cultural mindset and philosophical questions about reality influence artistic conventions and representational choices, leading to distinct artistic styles.
findings.quote: the general cultural climate affects the style of painting as well as the other arts.

findings.antecedent: Cross-cultural comparisons
findings.mechanism: By observing phenomena across diverse cultural groups, researchers can identify a wider range of perceptual variations and their underlying causes, leading to more general and complete theories than studies confined to Western cultures.
findings.quote: cross-cultural studies of real and represented space extend our understanding of perception primarily by demonstrating that the range of magnitude of the various phenomena is much greater than is suggested by studies conducted in Western cultures
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hudson (1960), Segall et al. (1963, 1966).

findings.antecedent: Cross-cultural comparisons
findings.consequent: Reordering of relative importance of psychological phenomena
findings.mechanism: By examining how different cultures prioritize or manifest various perceptual phenomena, cross-cultural studies can reveal new relationships and highlight phenomena previously considered marginal in Western psychology.
findings.quote: Cross-cultural comparisons reorder the relative importance of some psychological phenomena and the perceived relationships among them.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Illusions and pictorial perception generally treated separately in the West.

findings.antecedent: Pictures
findings.mechanism: Pictures vary fundamentally in how they convey three-dimensionality (2/3i vs. 2/3d), involving different perceptual processes and serving different representational functions.
findings.quote: Pictures should not be regarded as forming a unified category in which individual instances differ merely in the quality and quantity of the monocular cues
findings.empirical_support_cited: Blakemore (1973) on monocular cues.

findings.antecedent: 2/3i pictures
findings.mechanism: These images, which describe nature without directly evoking spatial illusion, likely served as early attempts to represent objects symbolically, forming a precursor to written language.
findings.quote: The former can be thought of as an attempt to describe nature and probably constituted a step towards pictographic writing
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fortes (1940, 1981) on Tallensi drawings.

findings.antecedent: 2/3d pictures
findings.mechanism: These images, by providing stimulation similar to that derived from real space and directly evoking spatial illusions, aim to create a realistic perceptual experience.
findings.quote: the latter is an attempt to imitate nature by providing a kind of stimulation similar to that derived from real space.

findings.antecedent: Models (figurines)
findings.mechanism: Models, being 3D stimuli, are more readily accepted and understood across cultures than 2D pictures, especially in tasks requiring recognition or spatial understanding, due to their inherent three-dimensionality.
findings.source: Author's Response, Perception of solid models, para 2
findings.quote: A model is therefore 'superior' to a picture
findings.empirical_support_cited: Deregowski (1968a) on Bisa schoolchildren, Deregowski & Serpell (1971) on sorting tasks, Klapper & Birch (1969), Sigel (1968).

findings.antecedent: Rotation of a figure (e.g., Figure 17)
findings.mechanism: Changing the orientation of a figure can alter the perceived spatial cues, leading observers to interpret a previously 3D-perceived object as a flat, 2D pattern, especially in cultures with specific pictorial conventions.
findings.quote: when the figure was rotated through 45 degrees so that it became symmetrical about a vertical axis, most of them built a 2D model.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Deregowski (1980b) on Scottish schoolchildren with Figure 17.

findings.antecedent: Nonpictorial activities (e.g., Kxoe Bushmen's traditional life)
findings.consequent: Skills relevant to picture perception (Region B skills)
findings.mechanism: Certain real-world activities and environmental interactions in a culture can develop perceptual skills that are transferable and beneficial for interpreting pictorial information, even if the culture has limited direct exposure to pictures.
findings.source: Author's Response, Perception of solid models, para 6
findings.quote: the nonpictorial activities of the Kxoe foster skills relevant to picture perception (i.e., their skills are those represented by area B in Figure 25).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bentley and Deregowski (1987) on Kxoe children.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: A desirable study... would be to compare performance on the 'two-pronged trident' task with performance on Street-type figures, which require the integration of pictorial elements but do not involve pictorial (2/3d) depth.
One might test the ability to interpret a picture viewed at an angle, a task investigated by Hagen (1976), Goldstein (1979), and Deregowski and Parker (1988).
Future research should try to disentangle the effects of complexity and conventions on performance.
bridge_warrants: Connects to Gibson's ecological approach (critiqued and refined).
Connects to Piagetian theory (Colomb & Dasen, Sigel).
Connects to Witkin's field dependence (constancy studies).
Connects to theories of art and aesthetic perception (Chwistek, Grigg).
Connects to theories of object recognition (Biederman's geons, Marr and Nishihara).
methodological_critiques: Hudson's test: 'admittedly poor in pictorial cues,' 'abbreviated series of stimuli,' 'grossly distorted,' 'ill advised' modifications (Hagen & Johnson), 'biased' by employer assessment (Dana & Voigt).
Segall et al. studies: 'do not unambiguously indicate that particular hypotheses should be rejected,' 'difficult to interpret unambiguously' due to genetic/environmental confounds.

General cross-cultural studies: 'inconsistent,' 'poorly documented,' 'may well involve factors other than those immediately associated with pictorial perception,' 'difficulties in matching samples from populations that differ both genetically and in their exposure to particular environments,' 'uncalled-for variable... drawings,' 'lack of appropriate findings.'
Training studies: 'not comprehensive,' 'effects of training are measured on the same kind of stimuli as those used in training.'
Illusion studies: 'not clear whether the observed effect is due to differences in the strength of the stimuli,' 'unrelated perceptual processes' for different illusion types.
It is unwise to rely on a single measure for such a broad concept as perception of picture space.
model_structure: The paper proposes a model (Figure 25) where spatial skills are divided into three categories: (1) 3D spatial skills exclusively used in the real world (e.g., binocular disparity, Region A), (2) representational skills exclusively used for pictures (e.g., interpreting multiple representations as movement, Region E), and (3) shared skills that can be used in both real and pictorial perception (e.g., interpreting overlap, Regions B, C, D). The extent of overlap and the specific skills acquired vary across cultures and influence picture perception.
limitations: Available data do not allow us to evaluate the relative magnitude of genetic and environmental contributions to perceptual skills.
Nor are data that could help to clarify some of these issues likely to become available.
The words culture and cultural repeatedly used here are not used in a purist sense.
It is impossible to determine to what extent test scores are a consequence of differential familiarity with pictorial materials or of differences in spatial ability.
It is uncertain to what extent the selection of those cues depends on genetic predispositions and to what extent it is acquired.
It would seem rash to maintain that learning does not occur. Nor would it be reasonable to postulate that that learning is of the 'all-or-none' variety.
The notion of skills used above is, of necessity, global and general. Elementary components of such skills have not been widely studied cross-culturally.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Real space and represented space: Cross-cultural perspectives
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThis paper examines the contribution of cross-cultural studies to our understanding of the perception and representation of space. A cross-cultural survey of the basic difficulties in understanding pictures—ranging from the failure to recognise a picture as a representation to the inability to recognise the object represented in the picture— indicates that similar difficulties occur in pictorial and nonpictorial cultrues. The experimental work on pictorial space derives from two distinct traditions: the study of picture perception in “remote” populations and the study of the perceptual illusions. A comprison of the findings on pictorial space perception with those on real space perceptual illusions. A comparison of findings on pictorial space perception with those on real space perception and perceptual constancy suggersts that cross-cultural differences in the perception of both real and representational space involve two different types of skills: those related exclusively to either real space or representational space, and those related to both. Different cultural groups use different skills to perform the same perceptual tasks.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Extends existing theories of spatial cognition by differentiating between real and represented space and exploring their cross-cultural variations.
Assumes that human minds actively construct and interpret spatial representations based on sensory input and cultural learning.
Proposes that cultural background significantly shapes the conventions and interpretations used in spatial representation and understanding.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper conceptually explores how pictorial representations of space are interpreted through cultural lenses and cognitive processes, thereby shaping or relating to an individual's understanding of real space.
